params.question: In heart failure, pulmonary oedema and orthopnoea are symptoms of forward failure caused by reduced cardiac output.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. Pulmonary oedema and orthopnoea arise from backward failure — elevated left-sided filling pressures transmitted to the pulmonary capillary bed cause fluid transudation into the interstitium and alveoli. Forward failure (reduced cardiac output) manifests as fatigue, exercise intolerance, and symptoms of poor tissue perfusion.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct! Pulmonary oedema and orthopnoea are manifestations of backward failure, not forward failure. Elevated left ventricular filling pressures transmit backward through the left atrium to the pulmonary veins, raising pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure and causing fluid transudation into the alveoli. Forward failure (reduced cardiac output) produces fatigue, exercise intolerance, and poor tissue perfusion.

params.question: A patient with suspected heart failure has a JVP elevated to the earlobes. Based on the governing principles discussed, which clinical conclusion can the examining clinician most reliably draw from this finding?

answers.text: Left ventricular ejection fraction is severely reduced

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The JVP reflects right atrial pressure, not left ventricular systolic function. LVEF requires echocardiographic assessment and cannot be inferred from JVP height alone.

Correct — the JVP is a direct haemodynamic window into right atrial pressure. A JVP elevated to the earlobes indicates markedly raised right atrial pressure, reflecting significant right-sided congestion.

Pulmonary oedema reflects backward failure of the left ventricle with elevated pulmonary capillary pressures. An elevated JVP reflects right-sided congestion — the two can coexist but are physiologically distinct findings.

answers.text: Infective endocarditis should be the primary suspicion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An elevated JVP indicates raised right atrial pressure from any cause — heart failure, pericardial disease, fluid overload, or pulmonary hypertension. It is not specific to infective endocarditis and should not be used alone to suspect IE.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. The JVP directly reflects right atrial pressure. A markedly elevated JVP indicates significant right-sided congestion and helps establish the severity of heart failure — this is the governing principle discussed in the video.

Correct! The JVP is a direct haemodynamic window into right atrial pressure — using each clinical sign as a window into the patient's haemodynamics is the governing principle of cardiovascular examination in heart failure.

interactions.label: Which of the following is NOT one of the four evidence-based pillar drug classes

params.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four evidence-based pillar drug classes in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ACEi/ARBs/ARNI form Pillar 1 of GDMT — they target the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, reducing vasoconstriction, lowering preload and afterload, and inhibiting pathological cardiac remodelling.
Beta-blockers form Pillar 2 of GDMT — they counteract the deleterious effects of chronic sympathetic overactivation, reducing heart rate, myocardial oxygen demand, and arrhythmia risk.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) form Pillar 3 of GDMT — they block aldosterone-mediated sodium retention, potassium wasting, and myocardial fibrosis.

Correct — loop diuretics relieve congestion symptoms but are NOT one of the four disease-modifying GDMT pillars. They do not reduce mortality or reverse ventricular remodelling, unlike the four pillars that target the neurohormonal cascade.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. Loop diuretics, though commonly used, are not one of the four GDMT pillars. The pillars are ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors — all targeting the neurohormonal cascade that drives disease progression.

Correct! Loop diuretics are essential for symptom relief in congestion but are not disease-modifying. The four GDMT pillars — each targeting a different aspect of the neurohormonal cascade — are what reduce mortality and reverse remodelling in HFrEF.

params.question: A 22-year-old presents with exertional dyspnoea. Echocardiography reveals a large atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunt. Which statement best explains why this patient is NOT cyanosed?

answers.text: The excess blood passing through the lungs is reoxygenated, maintaining overall oxygen saturation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While blood passing through the lungs is oxygenated, this does not explain the absence of cyanosis. The key is that in a left-to-right shunt, no deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation in the first place — it is the DIRECTION of shunting that determines cyanosis, not reoxygenation.

answers.text: Deoxygenated blood from the right atrium is diluted by the larger volume of oxygenated left atrial blood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dilution of deoxygenated by oxygenated blood would still produce some degree of desaturation. The fundamental reason for absence of cyanosis is that in a left-to-right shunt, blood only crosses from the oxygenated left side to the right — no deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation at all.

answers.text: Oxygenated blood from the left atrium crosses to the right heart, so systemic arterial blood remains fully saturated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — in a left-to-right shunt, oxygenated blood from the left atrium enters the right atrium and travels through the pulmonary circulation again. Critically, no deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation, so arterial oxygen saturation remains normal.

answers.text: Eisenmenger physiology has not yet developed, so the shunt direction has not reversed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Eisenmenger syndrome (shunt reversal due to pulmonary hypertension) would indeed cause cyanosis if it developed, but this does not explain why the current left-to-right shunt is inherently acyanotic. The absence of cyanosis is because oxygenated blood crosses from left to right, keeping systemic blood fully saturated.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. The key principle is shunt direction: in a left-to-right shunt, only oxygenated blood crosses to the right heart, so systemic arterial blood remains fully saturated. Cyanosis occurs only when deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation via a right-to-left shunt.

Correct! In left-to-right shunts, systemic arterial blood remains fully saturated because the shunted blood flows from the oxygenated left side to the right heart — the fundamental division between acyanotic and cyanotic congenital heart disease depends on shunt direction.
